newsitem.title: USA: Central U.S. looks poised for bitter cold weekend.
newsitem.headline: Central U.S. looks poised for bitter cold weekend.

text.p: Wheat growing areas in the Great Plains of the United States face a sharp drop in temperatures this weekend without much snow cover but it is not expected to be cold enough to do much damage, meteorologists said.

"Very cold air will be working its way into winter wheat areas during the weekend. It is unlikely to be cold enough to do any major damage but there will be little or no protective snow cover," Mike Palmerino of Weather Services Corp said.
He said temperatures in northwest Kansas could drop to minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit on either Sunday or Monday morning with lows in southwest Kansas around minus 5 F.
Palmerino noted that temperatures had already begun to fall during the last few days which should ensure the hard red winter wheat crop was dormant before the cold air hits.

Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis said extremely cold Arctic air was expected to produce lows on Saturday and Sunday around minus 15 to 20 F in Nebraska, minus 10 to 15 F in Kansas and minus 5 to 10 in Oklahoma and the Texas Panhandle.

"Since the vast majority of the (HRW wheat) belt does not have a protective snowcover, and is not expected to get one between now and then, some winterkill damage is possible," Davis wrote in this daily weather outlook.
WSC's Palmerino said some soft red winter wheat areas may, however, receive some snow protection prior to the weekend.

He said parts of central and southern Missouri could get between three and six inches of snow and ice late Wednesday and on Thursday and it was also possible that some crops in Ohio could receive some snow cover.
"The soft red crop is going to have more protection than the hard red crop," Palmerino said.
Cash grain merchandisers in Ohio noted the farmers were attempting to belatedly harvest soybeans and even some corn on Tuesday ahead of expected snowfall later this week.
Smith Barney's Davis said lows could drop down to zero F as far south as northern Missouri, central Illinois, central Indiana and central Ohio on Sunday or Monday morning.
"A widespread damage event is not expected since it is rare for a well established winter wheat crop to sustain severe damage during the middle of winter," Davis wrote.
Hog prices in the U.S. Midwest were mostly higher on Wednesday as packers rounded up as many hogs as possible before snow and severe cold move into the Midwest, livestock dealers said.
WSC's Palmerino said temperatures could drop as low as minus 10 F in Iowa on Sunday morning.
He noted that although temperatures would drop to well below normal levels, that was not unusual during winter.
"We normally see several events like this every winter," Palmerino said.
